first.title: How slice::first works
first.description: The first item, as an Option (None for an empty slice).

note.text: safe: no panic on an empty slice

slides.caption: first() looks at index 0 if there is one.
The slice is not empty, so index 0 exists: 7.
For [] it would return None, where v[0] would panic.
The result is a reference, &7, printed as 7. last() works the same way from the other end.

last.title: How slice::last works
last.description: The last item, as an Option (None for an empty slice).

slides.caption: last() looks at index len() - 1, if the slice is not empty.
The length is 3, so the last index is 2: 9.
Unlike Iterator::last, slice::last is instant: it goes straight to the end.

get.title: How slice::get works
get.description: Reads an index safely: Some(item), or None when it is out of range.

slides.caption: get is the safe version of v[i]: instead of panicking, it returns None.
There is no index 5 (the last index is 2): None, no panic.
Use v[i] when the index must be valid (a bug otherwise), and get(i) when it may not be.

contains.title: How slice::contains works
contains.description: Checks whether an equal item is in the slice.

slides.caption: contains compares each item with 7, from the front.
7 equals 7: true, and the search stops.
contains looks at items one by one. For many lookups in a big collection, a HashSet is much faster.

windows.title: How slice::windows works
windows.description: Every run of n neighbouring items; the windows overlap.

note.text: a window of 2 sliding one step

slides.caption: windows(2) looks at 2 items at a time and slides one step to the right each time.
It slides one step: [2, 3]. The 2 is used again.
[3, 4], and the window has reached the end.
A slice of length n gives n - size + 1 windows. Great for comparing neighbours: w[1] - w[0].

chunks.title: How slice::chunks works
chunks.description: Splits the slice into pieces of n items; the last piece may be shorter.

slides.caption: chunks(2) cuts the slice into consecutive pieces of 2.
[3, 4]. Unlike windows, no item is used twice.
Only 5 is left: the last chunk is just [5].
Use chunks_exact if every piece must have exactly n items; the leftovers are then available separately.

chunks_exact.title: How slice::chunks_exact works
chunks_exact.description: Pieces of exactly n items; leftovers are kept apart.

slides.caption: chunks_exact(2) yields only pieces of exactly 2 items.
5 cannot make a full piece: it is not yielded, but .remainder() returns it.
Because every chunk has the same length, the compiler can often make loops over chunks_exact faster.

split_at.title: How slice::split_at works
split_at.description: Divides a slice into two at an index; nothing is copied.

slides.caption: split_at(1) returns two views of the same memory: before index 1, and from index 1 on.
The left part ends just before index 1: [1].
The right part starts at index 1: [2, 3, 4].
Both parts borrow the original slice. An index past the end panics; split_at_checked returns an Option instead.

split_first.title: How slice::split_first works
split_first.description: The first item and the rest, or None if the slice is empty.

slides.caption: split_first separates the first item from the others.
Handy in recursive code: if let Some((first, rest)) = s.split_first() { ... }.

binary_search.title: How slice::binary_search works
binary_search.description: Finds an item in a sorted slice by halving the search range each step.

slides.caption: binary_search never looks at every item. It checks the middle and throws away the half that cannot contain 9.
The middle is 7. 9 > 7, so 9 can only be in the right half.
The middle of what is left is 9: found at index 4.
If the item is missing, the result is Err(index where it would go): searching 4 gives Err(2). On an unsorted slice the result is meaningless.

binary_search_by_key.title: How slice::binary_search_by_key works
binary_search_by_key.description: Binary search on a key of each item; the slice must be sorted by that key.

slides.caption: binary_search_by_key compares the key (here the age, p.1) instead of the whole item.
The middle person, bo, is 30: that is the age searched for.
The slice must be sorted by the same key, for example with sort_by_key(|p| p.1).

partition_point.title: How slice::partition_point works
partition_point.description: The index of the first item for which the test becomes false.

slides.caption: All items that pass the test must come first. partition_point finds the border with a binary search.
1, 2 and 3 are < 5: they are before the border.
7 is the first item that is not < 5, at index 3.
partition_point is the insertion index: v.insert(3, 5) keeps the slice sorted.

sort_unstable.title: How slice::sort_unstable works
sort_unstable.description: Sorts in place, fast; equal items may change order.

slides.caption: sort_unstable rearranges the items inside the slice from smallest to largest.
1 is the smallest: it goes first.
"Unstable" only means equal items may swap places. For plain numbers that is invisible, and it is faster than sort().

sort_unstable_by_key.title: How slice::sort_unstable_by_key works
sort_unstable_by_key.description: Sorts by a computed key, in place.

slides.caption: The closure gives each item a key (its length); the items are ordered by those keys.
Use sort_by_key instead if words with the same length must keep their original order.

reverse.title: How slice::reverse works
reverse.description: Reverses the order of the items in place.

slides.caption: reverse swaps the first and last item, then the second and second-to-last, until it meets in the middle.
2 and 3 trade places. The middle is reached.
reverse changes the slice itself. To read backwards without changing anything, use iter().rev().

rotate_left.title: How slice::rotate_left works
rotate_left.description: Shifts every item n places left; the ones that fall off the front go to the back.

slides.caption: rotate_left(2) moves everything 2 places to the left. The first 2 items wrap around to the end.
1 and 2 fell off the front, so they go to the back.
rotate_right(2) does the opposite: [4, 5, 1, 2, 3]. No items are lost or copied.

swap.title: How slice::swap works
swap.description: Exchanges the items at two indexes.

slides.caption: swap(0, 2) trades the items at index 0 and index 2.
You cannot write std::mem::swap(&mut v[0], &mut v[2]) (two mutable borrows of v), which is why slices have their own swap.

starts_with.title: How slice::starts_with works
starts_with.description: Checks whether the slice begins with the given items.

slides.caption: starts_with compares the first items of the slice with the prefix, in order.
ends_with checks the back the same way. An empty prefix always matches.

fill.title: How slice::fill works
fill.description: Overwrites every item with the same value.

slides.caption: fill(0) writes 0 into every place of the slice.
Works on part of a slice too: v[1..].fill(0) gives [1, 0, 0].

iter.title: How slice::iter works
iter.description: An iterator over references to the items; the slice stays usable.

title.text: for x in v.iter() { ... }   // v = vec![1, 2, 3]

slides.caption: iter() lends out each item as a reference, &i32. The Vec keeps ownership.
x is &1: a reference to the first item.
After the loop, v can still be used: nothing was moved out.
for x in &v is the same as for x in v.iter(). Use iter_mut() to change items, into_iter() to take them.

ends_with.title: How slice::ends_with works
ends_with.description: Checks whether the slice ends with the given items.

slides.caption: ends_with lines the suffix up with the end of the slice.
The 1 at the front does not matter.

rotate_right.title: How slice::rotate_right works
rotate_right.description: Shifts every item n places right; the ones at the end wrap around to the front.

note.text: the last item comes to the front

slides.caption: rotate_right(1) moves every item one place right.
4 falls off the end and wraps around to the front.

split.title: How slice::split works
split.description: Cuts a slice at every item that matches; the matches are dropped.

slides.caption: split works like str::split, but for any slice.
After the last 0: [4]. The zeros themselves are not in any piece.
Each piece borrows the original slice: nothing is copied.

iter_mut.title: How slice::iter_mut works
iter_mut.description: An iterator of mutable references, to change items in place.

slides.caption: iter_mut lends out each item as &mut, so the loop can change it.
for x in &mut v is the same thing. The * is needed because x is a reference.

split_last.title: How slice::split_last works
split_last.description: The last item and everything before it.

slides.caption: split_last separates the final item from the others.

rchunks.title: How slice::rchunks works
rchunks.description: Like chunks, but starting from the end.

note.text: the short piece is at the front

slides.caption: rchunks cuts pieces of 2 from the back.
Useful for grouping digits from the right, like thousands separators.

chunk_by.title: How slice::chunk_by works
chunk_by.description: Splits a slice into runs where neighbours satisfy a test.

slides.caption: chunk_by compares each item with the next; a false starts a new piece.
Group equal neighbours with chunk_by(|a, b| a == b).

binary_search_by.title: How slice::binary_search_by works
binary_search_by.description: Binary search with your own comparison.

slides.caption: The closure says how each item compares to what you are looking for.
Return Less, Equal or Greater from the closure; for floats use total_cmp.

select_nth_unstable.title: How slice::select_nth_unstable works
select_nth_unstable.description: Puts the n-th smallest item in place n, faster than a full sort.

slides.caption: After the call, v[2] is what it would be if v were sorted; smaller items are before it, larger after it.
Runs in linear time on average: ideal for medians and percentiles.

is_sorted.title: How slice::is_sorted works
is_sorted.description: Checks that each item is at most the next one.

slides.caption: is_sorted compares every pair of neighbours.
All pairs are in order: true.
Check this before binary_search in debug code: debug_assert!(v.is_sorted()).

get_mut.title: How slice::get_mut works
get_mut.description: Borrows one item mutably if the index exists.

slides.caption: get_mut is the &mut version of get: Some(&mut item) or None.
v[1] = 20 does the same but panics for a bad index.

copy_from_slice.title: How slice::copy_from_slice works
copy_from_slice.description: Overwrites a slice with the items of another slice of the same length.

slides.caption: copy_from_slice copies item by item into the target range.
The target is buf[1..3], two places.
Different lengths panic. clone_from_slice works for non-Copy items.

split_inclusive.title: How slice::split_inclusive works
split_inclusive.description: Like split, but each separator stays at the end of its piece.

slides.caption: Each piece ends with the item that matched.
str has split_inclusive too, handy for keeping line endings.

fill_with.title: How slice::fill_with works
fill_with.description: Fills every place with the result of a closure.

title.text: let mut n = 0; v.fill_with(|| { n += 1; n * n });

slides.caption: fill_with calls the closure once per place.
fill(x) copies one value everywhere; fill_with can make each one different.

len.title: How slice::len works
len.description: The number of elements in a slice or array.

slides.caption: len counts elements, whatever their size.
Valid indexes go from 0 to len - 1. For a str, len counts bytes instead.

is_empty.title: How slice::is_empty works
is_empty.description: true if the slice has no elements.

slides.caption: Clippy suggests is_empty whenever you write len() == 0.

first_mut.title: How slice::first_mut works
first_mut.description: A mutable reference to the first element, or None if empty.

slides.caption: first_mut never panics; v[0] would on an empty Vec.
last_mut does the same for the end.

last_mut.title: How slice::last_mut works
last_mut.description: A mutable reference to the last element, or None if empty.

slides.caption: Typical for building output: change the last line you added.
Returns None for an empty slice.

split_at_mut.title: How slice::split_at_mut works
split_at_mut.description: Two non-overlapping mutable halves of one slice.

slides.caption: Rust forbids two &mut to the same Vec, but two &mut to separate halves are fine.
The standard way around "cannot borrow v as mutable more than once".

get_disjoint_mut.title: How slice::get_disjoint_mut works
get_disjoint_mut.description: Several mutable references at chosen indexes, checked to be different.

slides.caption: It returns Err if an index repeats or is out of bounds.
HashMap::get_disjoint_mut does the same with keys.
Each piece between separators is lent mutably in turn.
The separators themselves are not part of any piece.

swap_with_slice.title: How slice::swap_with_slice works
swap_with_slice.description: Exchanges all elements with another slice of the same length.

slides.caption: Both slices must be exactly as long.

clone_from_slice.title: How slice::clone_from_slice works
clone_from_slice.description: Overwrites every element with a clone from another slice.

slides.caption: Like copy_from_slice, but works for Strings and other Clone types.
"x" is replaced by a clone of "a".

rsplit.title: How slice::rsplit works
rsplit.description: Pieces between separators, from the end backwards.

slides.caption: Same pieces as split, in reverse order.

splitn.title: How slice::splitn works
splitn.description: Splits at separators, into at most n pieces.

slides.caption: After n - 1 cuts, the rest stays together.
The rest is one piece, with its 0 inside.
rsplitn counts the cuts from the end.

rsplitn.title: How slice::rsplitn works
rsplitn.description: Splits from the end, into at most n pieces.

slides.caption: The last separator splits off the tail; the rest stays whole.
Good for "everything before the last delimiter".

chunks_mut.title: How slice::chunks_mut works
chunks_mut.description: Mutable pieces of a fixed size (the last may be shorter).

slides.caption: Each chunk is lent mutably in turn.
Image code uses it to process one row of pixels at a time.

chunks_exact_mut.title: How slice::chunks_exact_mut works
chunks_exact_mut.description: Mutable chunks of exactly n elements; leftovers are skipped.

slides.caption: The 5 does not fill a chunk, so it is not visited.
Their first items become 0; 5 is untouched.

rchunks_exact.title: How slice::rchunks_exact works
rchunks_exact.description: Full chunks counted from the end; the leftover is at the start.

slides.caption: 1 is the remainder because the chunks are counted from the right.
Grouping digits in threes from the right: 1,234,567.

sort_unstable_by.title: How slice::sort_unstable_by works
sort_unstable_by.description: Fast in-place sort with your own comparison; equal items may change order.

slides.caption: "Unstable" only means that equal elements may swap places; the result is still sorted.
Usually faster than sort_by and uses no extra memory.

select_nth_unstable_by_key.title: How slice::select_nth_unstable_by_key works
select_nth_unstable_by_key.description: Puts the element with the n-th smallest key at index n.

slides.caption: Only position n is guaranteed; the others are just on the correct side.
The smallest key, "a", goes to index 0.
Faster than sorting when you need one rank, e.g. a median.

strip_prefix.title: How slice::strip_prefix works
strip_prefix.description: The rest of the slice after a given beginning, or None.

slides.caption: If the slice starts with the prefix, you get what comes after it.
strip_suffix does the same at the end.

strip_suffix.title: How slice::strip_suffix works
strip_suffix.description: The slice without a given ending, or None if it does not end that way.

slides.caption: Only an exact match at the end counts.
Returns None if the ending is different.

copy_within.title: How slice::copy_within works
copy_within.description: Copies a range of the slice to another position in the same slice.

slides.caption: Elements 0..2 are copied so that they start at index 3.
Works like memmove; only for Copy types.

first_chunk.title: How slice::first_chunk works
first_chunk.description: The first N elements as a fixed-size array reference.

title.text: let Some(&[a, b]) = v.first_chunk::<2>() else { return };

slides.caption: The size is checked once, and you get a real array you can destructure.
last_chunk takes them from the end. Handy for reading fixed-size headers.

as_chunks.title: How slice::as_chunks works
as_chunks.description: Splits a slice into arrays of N elements plus a remainder.

slides.caption: Every chunk is a real [T; 2], so the compiler knows its size.
as_rchunks puts the remainder at the start instead.

split_first_chunk.title: How slice::split_first_chunk works
split_first_chunk.description: The first N elements as an array, plus the rest of the slice.

slides.caption: Ideal for binary formats: a fixed header followed by data.
The header is the first 2 bytes.
Returns None if the slice is shorter than N.

select_nth_unstable_by.title: How slice::select_nth_unstable_by works
select_nth_unstable_by.description: Like select_nth_unstable, with your own comparison.

slides.caption: Floats have no Ord, so you pass the comparison.

is_ascii.title: How [u8]::is_ascii works
is_ascii.description: true if every byte is below 128.

slides.caption: é is stored as two bytes above 127.
str::is_ascii does the same on a string.

eq_ignore_ascii_case.title: How [u8]::eq_ignore_ascii_case works
eq_ignore_ascii_case.description: Compares two byte strings, ignoring the case of ASCII letters.

slides.caption: Each pair of bytes is compared after lower-casing.
Common when parsing protocols like HTTP.
Only a–z change; other bytes stay as they are.
o and k become O and K.
to_ascii_uppercase returns a new Vec<u8> instead.

trim_ascii.title: How [u8]::trim_ascii works
trim_ascii.description: Removes ASCII whitespace from both ends of a byte slice.

slides.caption: Like str::trim, but for raw bytes.
Leading spaces and the trailing space and newline go.
trim_ascii_start and trim_ascii_end do one side.

escape_ascii.title: How [u8]::escape_ascii works
escape_ascii.description: Shows bytes as readable text, escaping anything unprintable.

slides.caption: Printable ASCII is kept; newlines and other bytes become escapes.
Safer than from_utf8_lossy when you want to see the exact bytes.

next.title: How next works on a slice iterator
next.description: Gives the next element of v.iter(), or None at the end.

slides.caption: The iterator keeps a position; each next() moves it forward.
A for loop calls next() for you until it returns None.

next_back.title: How next_back works on a slice iterator
next_back.description: Takes the next element from the end.

slides.caption: Slice iterators can be consumed from both ends.
The last element comes out first.
rev() uses next_back to walk backwards.

any.title: How any works on v.iter()
any.description: true if at least one element passes the test; stops at the first one.

slides.caption: any checks elements in order and stops as soon as one passes.
An empty slice gives false. 1 is never looked at.

all.title: How all works on v.iter()
all.description: true if every element passes the test; stops at the first failure.

slides.caption: all stops as soon as one element fails.
An empty slice gives true: nothing fails.

find.title: How find works on v.iter()
find.description: The first element that passes the test, as Some(&x).

slides.caption: find returns a reference to the element, or None.
Use position() if you need the index instead.

find_map.title: How find_map works on v.iter()
find_map.description: Applies a function until it returns Some, and gives that value.

slides.caption: Like find, but you also transform the element.

position.title: How position works on v.iter()
position.description: The index of the first element that passes the test.

slides.caption: Counts from 0 and stops at the first match.
rposition searches from the end: it would give 3.

rposition.title: How rposition works on v.iter()
rposition.description: The index of the last element that passes the test.

slides.caption: Searches backwards but still reports the normal index.

count.title: How count works on v.iter()
count.description: How many elements are left; instant for slices.

slides.caption: A slice iterator knows its length, so count does not loop.
v.len() is the simpler way; count() is useful after filter().

nth.title: How nth works on v.iter()
nth.description: Skips n elements and returns the next one (0 = first).

slides.caption: For slices nth jumps directly; it does not step one by one.
The skipped elements are consumed: a second nth(0) would be None here.

nth_back.title: How nth_back works on v.iter()
nth_back.description: Skips n elements from the end and returns the next one.

slides.caption: Counting from the end: 4 is position 0, 3 is position 1.
v.get(v.len() - 2) gives the same element without an iterator.

slice_iter-last.title: How last works on v.iter()
slice_iter-last.description: The last element, without walking through the others.

slides.caption: Slice iterators go straight to the end.
The end of the slice is 9.
v.last() does the same on the slice itself.

fold.title: How fold works on v.iter()
fold.description: Combines all elements into one value, starting from an initial value.

slides.caption: fold carries an accumulator through every element.
sum() and product() are special cases of fold.

for_each.title: How for_each works on v.iter()
for_each.description: Runs a closure on every element.

slides.caption: for_each is the method form of a for loop.
Each element is passed to the closure.
A for loop is usually clearer; for_each reads well at the end of a chain.
Each window is a slice that borrows from v.

windows_iter-count.title: How Windows::count works
windows_iter-count.description: How many windows fit: len - size + 1.

slides.caption: If the size is larger than the slice, count is 0.
Same as v[v.len() - 2..] when it exists.

chunks_iter-next.title: How Chunks::next works
chunks_iter-next.description: Gives the next piece of up to n elements.

chunks_iter-count.title: How Chunks::count works
chunks_iter-count.description: How many chunks: len divided by n, rounded up.

split_first_mut.title: How slice::split_first_mut works
split_first_mut.description: The first element and the rest, both mutable.

slides.caption: head and rest do not overlap, so both can be changed.

split_last_mut.title: How slice::split_last_mut works
split_last_mut.description: The last element and everything before it, both mutable.

slides.caption: Here last becomes the sum of the others: 1 + 2 = 3.

split_at_checked.title: How slice::split_at_checked works
split_at_checked.description: split_at that returns None instead of panicking.

split_at_mut_checked.title: How slice::split_at_mut_checked works
split_at_mut_checked.description: split_at_mut that returns None instead of panicking.

title.text: if let Some((a, b)) = v.split_at_mut_checked(1) { a[0] = b[1]; }

slides.caption: None when the index is past the end.

split_inclusive_mut.title: How slice::split_inclusive_mut works
split_inclusive_mut.description: Mutable pieces that each end with their separator.

rsplit_mut.title: How slice::rsplit_mut works
rsplit_mut.description: Mutable pieces between separators, from the end.

slides.caption: The first piece yielded is the last one.

splitn_mut.title: How slice::splitn_mut works
splitn_mut.description: Mutable pieces between separators, at most n of them.

slides.caption: rsplitn_mut counts the cuts from the end.

rsplitn_mut.title: How slice::rsplitn_mut works
rsplitn_mut.description: Mutable pieces from the end, at most n of them.

rchunks_mut.title: How slice::rchunks_mut works
rchunks_mut.description: Mutable chunks counted from the end.

rchunks_exact_mut.title: How slice::rchunks_exact_mut works
rchunks_exact_mut.description: Full mutable chunks from the end; the leftover at the start is skipped.

slides.caption: First element of each chunk becomes 0.

chunk_by_mut.title: How slice::chunk_by_mut works
chunk_by_mut.description: Mutable runs of neighbours that pass a test.

title.text: for run in v.chunk_by_mut(|a, b| a == b) { run.fill(run.len() as i32); }

slides.caption: Runs: [1, 1] and [2, 2, 2]; each is filled with its length.

is_sorted_by.title: How slice::is_sorted_by works
is_sorted_by.description: Checks the order of neighbours with your own rule.

slides.caption: The closure says whether a may come before b.

is_sorted_by_key.title: How slice::is_sorted_by_key works
is_sorted_by_key.description: Checks that a key from each element never decreases.

last_chunk.title: How slice::last_chunk works
last_chunk.description: The last N elements as a fixed-size array.

slides.caption: The compiler knows the result has exactly N elements.
first_chunk takes them from the start.

first_chunk_mut.title: How slice::first_chunk_mut works
first_chunk_mut.description: The first N elements as a mutable array.

slides.caption: Gives &mut [T; N], so array methods work.

split_last_chunk.title: How slice::split_last_chunk works
split_last_chunk.description: Everything before, plus the last N elements as an array.

slides.caption: Good for formats that end with a fixed-size trailer.
The last byte is the trailer.
None if the slice is shorter than N.

as_rchunks.title: How slice::as_rchunks works
as_rchunks.description: A remainder at the start, then arrays of N elements.

slides.caption: Chunks are counted from the end.
as_chunks puts the remainder at the end.

as_flattened.title: How slice::as_flattened works
as_flattened.description: Views a slice of arrays as one flat slice.

slides.caption: No copying: the memory already lies flat.

make_ascii_lowercase.title: How [u8]::make_ascii_lowercase works
make_ascii_lowercase.description: Lower-cases ASCII letters in a byte slice, in place.

slides.caption: H, T, T, P become small.
to_ascii_lowercase returns a new Vec instead.

as_slice.title: How slice::Iter::as_slice works
as_slice.description: The part of the slice the iterator has not reached yet.

title.text: let mut it = v.iter(); it.next(); it.as_slice()

slides.caption: Borrowed straight from the original slice.

into_slice.title: How slice::IterMut::into_slice works
into_slice.description: Turns the iterator into a mutable slice of what is left.

title.text: let mut it = v.iter_mut(); it.next(); it.into_slice()[0] = 9;

slides.caption: The iterator is consumed; you get &mut to the remaining part.
The rest starts at 2, which becomes 9.
as_slice only borrows the rest immutably.

slice_iter_mut-as_slice.title: How slice::IterMut::as_slice works
slice_iter_mut-as_slice.description: Looks at the remaining elements of a mutable iterator.

title.text: let mut it = v.iter_mut(); it.next(); it.as_slice()

slides.caption: A shared view of what has not been handed out yet.
The iterator can still be used afterwards.

remainder.title: How ChunksExact::remainder works
remainder.description: The leftover elements that do not fill a whole chunk.

slides.caption: chunks_exact skips the short piece; remainder hands it to you.
Process full blocks fast, then handle the tail separately.

rchunks_exact-remainder.title: How RChunksExact::remainder works
rchunks_exact-remainder.description: The leftover at the start when chunking from the end.

slides.caption: Full chunks are taken from the right, so the start is left over.
Digit grouping: the first group may be short.

into_remainder.title: How ChunksExactMut::into_remainder works
into_remainder.description: A mutable reference to the leftover elements.

slides.caption: The iterator is consumed and gives &mut to the tail.
remainder() would only lend it immutably.

as_chunks_mut.title: How slice::as_chunks_mut works
as_chunks_mut.description: Mutable arrays of N elements, plus a mutable remainder.

title.text: let (pairs, _) = v.as_chunks_mut::<2>(); for p in pairs { p.swap(0, 1); }

as_flattened_mut.title: How slice::as_flattened_mut works
as_flattened_mut.description: Views a slice of arrays as one flat mutable slice.

slides.caption: No copying; the rows are already laid out flat.
The two rows become one slice of 4.
Handy for clearing image or matrix data.

last_chunk_mut.title: How slice::last_chunk_mut works
last_chunk_mut.description: The last N elements as a mutable array.

slides.caption: None if the slice is shorter than N.

split_first_chunk_mut.title: How slice::split_first_chunk_mut works
split_first_chunk_mut.description: The first N elements as a mutable array, and the mutable rest.

slides.caption: Header and body can be changed separately.
The header records the body length.
Useful for binary formats with a length prefix.

split_last_chunk_mut.title: How slice::split_last_chunk_mut works
split_last_chunk_mut.description: The mutable rest, and the last N elements as a mutable array.

slides.caption: Here the trailer becomes a checksum of the body.
None if the slice is too short.
Like windows(2), but each window is a [T; 2] you can destructure.
The size N is inferred from the pattern.

trim_ascii_start.title: How [u8]::trim_ascii_start works
trim_ascii_start.description: Removes ASCII whitespace from the start of a byte slice.

trim_ascii_end.title: How [u8]::trim_ascii_end works
trim_ascii_end.description: Removes ASCII whitespace from the end of a byte slice.

slides.caption: Handy after reading a line as bytes.

from_ref.title: How slice::from_ref works
from_ref.description: Turns a reference to one value into a slice of length 1.

slides.caption: No copy: the slice points at the same value.
Pass a single value to a function that wants a slice.

from_mut.title: How slice::from_mut works
from_mut.description: Turns a mutable reference to one value into a mutable slice of length 1.

slides.caption: Rarely needed, but avoids building a Vec.

as_ptr.title: How slice::as_ptr works
as_ptr.description: A raw pointer to the first element of a slice.

slides.caption: The slice must outlive the pointer.

as_ptr_range.title: How slice::as_ptr_range works
as_ptr_range.description: The start and one-past-the-end pointers of a slice.

slides.caption: Handy for checking whether a pointer lies inside the slice.
The end pointer must not be read.

get_unchecked.title: How slice::get_unchecked works
get_unchecked.description: An element without a bounds check (unsafe).

slides.caption: Out of range is undefined behaviour.

get_unchecked_mut.title: How slice::get_unchecked_mut works
get_unchecked_mut.description: A mutable element without a bounds check (unsafe).

slides.caption: Only for indexes known to be valid.

get_disjoint_unchecked_mut.title: How slice::get_disjoint_unchecked_mut works
get_disjoint_unchecked_mut.description: Several mutable elements by index, without checking that they differ (unsafe).

slides.caption: Duplicate or invalid indexes are undefined behaviour.

as_chunks_unchecked.title: How slice::as_chunks_unchecked works
as_chunks_unchecked.description: Views a slice as arrays of N, when the length is an exact multiple (unsafe).

as_chunks_unchecked_mut.title: How slice::as_chunks_unchecked_mut works
as_chunks_unchecked_mut.description: Mutable arrays of N from a slice whose length is a multiple of N (unsafe).

as_rchunks_mut.title: How slice::as_rchunks_mut works
as_rchunks_mut.description: A mutable remainder at the start, then mutable arrays of N.

slides.caption: Chunks are counted from the end.
The leftover is the first element.

as_array.title: How slice::as_array works
as_array.description: The slice as &[T; N] if the length is exactly N.

as_mut_array.title: How slice::as_mut_array works
as_mut_array.description: The slice as &mut [T; N] if the length is exactly N.

slides.caption: Then array methods work in place.

as_mut_ptr.title: How slice::as_mut_ptr works
as_mut_ptr.description: A raw mutable pointer to the first element.

slides.caption: Valid while the slice is alive and unmoved.

as_mut_ptr_range.title: How slice::as_mut_ptr_range works
as_mut_ptr_range.description: The start and one-past-the-end mutable pointers of a slice.

slides.caption: Walk from start to end with raw pointers.
Do not write at end itself.

align_to.title: How slice::align_to works
align_to.description: Splits a slice into a prefix, a middle of a larger aligned type, and a suffix (unsafe).

slides.caption: The middle must be valid as the new type.
Writes through the middle change the bytes.

element_offset.title: How slice::element_offset works
element_offset.description: The index of an element reference within the slice, if it belongs to it.

slides.caption: None for references outside the slice.

subslice_range.title: How slice::subslice_range works
subslice_range.description: The index range of a sub-slice within the slice, if it belongs to it.

slides.caption: str::substr_range does the same for text.

strip_circumfix.title: How slice::strip_circumfix works
strip_circumfix.description: Removes a given prefix and suffix together, if both are there.

slides.caption: None if either end does not match.

split_off.title: How slice::split_off works
split_off.description: Cuts a range off the front or back of a slice reference and returns it.

slides.caption: The range must touch one end of the slice.

split_off_mut.title: How slice::split_off_mut works
split_off_mut.description: Cuts a mutable range off one end of a &mut slice.

split_off_first.title: How slice::split_off_first works
split_off_first.description: Removes and returns the first element of a slice reference.

split_off_last.title: How slice::split_off_last works
split_off_last.description: Removes and returns the last element of a slice reference.

split_off_first_mut.title: How slice::split_off_first_mut works
split_off_first_mut.description: Removes the first element of a &mut slice and returns it mutably.

split_off_last_mut.title: How slice::split_off_last_mut works
split_off_last_mut.description: Removes the last element of a &mut slice and returns it mutably.

from_raw_parts.title: How slice::from_raw_parts works
from_raw_parts.description: Builds a &[T] from a pointer and a length (unsafe).

slides.caption: You guarantee the memory is valid, initialised and not mutated meanwhile.
Typical when receiving buffers from C.

from_raw_parts_mut.title: How slice::from_raw_parts_mut works
from_raw_parts_mut.description: Builds a &mut [T] from a pointer and a length (unsafe).

slides.caption: No other access may happen meanwhile.

rchunks_exact_mut-into_remainder.title: How RChunksExactMut::into_remainder works
rchunks_exact_mut-into_remainder.description: The mutable leftover at the start when chunking from the end.

slides.caption: Full chunks are taken from the right.
